units.text: Executive summary. DeepGrid Semi sells the certification stamp, not the autonomy dream. MoRTH GSR 184(E), live April 2026, mandates certified ADAS on every new N2/N3 commercial truck sold in India — a regulatory demand floor across a 5M+ truck base. The AD2 kit prices at ₹2.3L (₹2–2.5L band) PLAN against imports at ₹6.5L (Mobileye EyeQ6) to ₹15L (Nvidia Orin) — a ~2.8–6.5× gap ASSUMPTION ARITHMETIC PLAN . Owning the compute (28nm die, packaged part ₹1,750 ) lets us hold that price while gross margin expands from 45% (FPGA phase, FY27) to ~72% in the ASIC phase. Three stacked motions run on one hardware platform: (1) fleet retrofit kits now — no regulatory gate, revenue from day one; (2) OEM/Tier-1 line-fit for the mandate channel — the volume engine, entered after AIS-162/188 certification; (3) privateland driverless at ports, mines and plant yards — sold as per-vehicle-per-month software at 90%+ gross margin. The first retrofit customers are plant operators with private yards: one logo carries the kit sale, the data flywheel, and the future driverless contract. Primary planning numbers, from the working model (Business Plan v2.2): ADAS segment revenue ₹914 Cr at FY32 inside a company total of ₹1,388 Cr, with EBITDA breakeven in FY2028. Traction today: ₹1.01 Cr defence revenue CONTRACTED MEASURED ; AD0-class perception proven on FPGA (40 fps YOLOv11n ).

units.text: Second: government/PSU/defence (§3 Customer 2); the GeM record CONTRACTED opens doors. Third — the mandate channel, reframed as upside, not a committed date. OEM/Tier-1 design-in is relationship-gated: comparable regulation-created hardware markets (EU tachograph, eCall) show mandate volume normally flows to whichever supplier already has OEM relationships and homologation experience, not the cheapest new entrant — those incumbents typically absorbed aftermarket share within ~18 months once line-fit normalized EXTERNAL REFERENCE . This plan therefore pursues OEM/Tier-1 engagement opportunistically from month one (a) AIS-162/188 certification (T2-funded, §9) PLAN , (b) retrofit field- hours and Indian-road data as validation, (c) the T2 milestone clock (§9) — but does not treat a signed design-in as a required, dated event the way §8's revenue trajectory implicitly assumes. The pitch leads with capability, not price: owning perception + compute + model on Jiyu's <100 ms ASIL-D EHB lets us certify a single photon-to-brake latency number no mix-and-match integration can produce — but that pitch needs an actual OEM contact, which this plan does not yet have (§10 risk 10).

units.title: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: …
units.text: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: certification, tapeout and first OEM engagement all land inside 12–18 months. Comparable mandatedriven hardware markets have historically taken 3–5 years to move from mandate announcement to stable incumbent share EXTERNAL REFERENCE . In the slow case, FY27– FY29 revenue rests almost entirely on government/defence and insurer-co-funded retrofit (this section) while certification and OEM engagement continue in the background with no committed date — the fast case is upside, not the base the company should be funded against. The three phases are the spine of this plan, so they are set out as a matrix rather than described in prose. Read Figure 8 as the answer to four questions per phase: who we sell to, through whom, at what price, and what has to be true before the next phase opens.

units.text: The uncomfortable reading, kept in deliberately. Against imports we are three times cheaper. Against the device that actually wins mandated volume in India we are twenty times more expensive. Both statements are true, and a serious investor will find the second one. Our answer has to be that we are not selling into the same job: a ₹5,000 box satisfies an inspector, while our kit is what an OEM can put on a production line and a fleet can build a safety case on. That answer only holds if (a) enforcement eventually becomes real, (b) we win OEM line-fit, and (c) we field a stripped SKU for the segment that only wants compliance (§6). If none of those three lands, the low end takes the mandate and we are left with the organised segment alone. Moat, in order of durability: 1. Structural price floor: owned silicon at <$3–4/bare die (₹1,750 packaged, §5) makes the ₹2.3L price ours to hold; importers cannot follow down without destroying their own margin stack. 2. Certification + sovereignty: claimed only-indigenous AIS-validated chipset, AIS-004 native, 15 patents filed; foreign silicon excluded from government/defence fleets (§2). Certification is a path, not held — the killer risk, §10. 3. Data moat that compounds — narrower than it sounds.

The D100 chiplet turns the same DGrid Alpha tapeout into military-grade compute — lockstep RISC-V safety cores (ASIL-D path), AES-256 secure enclave — at zero additional design cost. W HY F LIG HT CONT ROL + V IO + AI MUS T LIV E ON ONE CHIP FC — Fly VIO — Know Where You Are AI — See & Decide The flight-control loop keeps the drone in the air — real-time, deterministic, every millisecond. It cannot wait on another chip. GPS is jammed along the LoC/LAC and never works indoors. Visual-inertial navigation is the only positioning that survives — geometry, not GPS. Onboard detection and obstacle avoidance when the comms link is gone — the drone must think for itself, on the drone. Fused on one die, they become a hardware fail-safe: when the link or GPS fails, the FC loop reads VIO position directly — same silicon, same clock, no bus, no second board — and flies itself home. Split across chips, that path gains latency, weight, power and failure points; a drone falling over a city or into stacked inventory is a lawsuit.

units.title: Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads
units.text: The commercial autonomous vehicle (AV) and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) semiconductor market is characterized by structural capital intensity, prolonged design-in validation cycles, and significant cash burn before achieving commercial viability1. Within this high-barrier landscape, DeepGrid Semi, currently incubated at T-Hub Phase 2 in Hyderabad, stands at a critical technological and commercial crossroads1. As an early-stage, pre-revenue fabless semiconductor startup, DeepGrid has successfully validated its custom INT8 edge-AI architecture on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)1. However, the enterprise currently lacks established Tier-1 automotive customers or the massive capital required to transition from high-cost FPGA prototyping—which currently costs approximately () per board—to mass-produced custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), projected to cost less than () per chip at scale1. To fund the physical fabrication of its custom combo-die, DeepGrid is actively seeking to raise a () Pre-Series A venture capital round1. For institutional investors, technical validation on FPGAs is insufficient; the primary investment thesis depends on demonstrating a realistic, rapid path to commercial traction and cash-flow generation1.

units.text: This report establishes a systematic framework for identifying DeepGrid’s Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs) and maps out actionable Go-To-Market (GTM) strategies customized to these profiles1. By analyzing the commercial playbooks of global autonomous vehicle leaders and domestic Indian semiconductor startups, this report outlines how DeepGrid can leverage near-term regulatory safety mandates, dual-use tactical contracts, and unique hardware price advantages to bypass traditional multi-year automotive OEM cycles, mitigate capital burn, and build a highly defensible, localized data moat in India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets1.

units.title: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
units.text: A common point of failure for fabless semiconductor startups is targeting broad, unconstrained market segments without evaluating customer buying behaviors, technical integration friction, and regulatory timelines1. To optimize its limited Pre-Series A capital, DeepGrid must utilize a rigorous, multi-dimensional diagnostic framework to identify, score, and prioritize potential customer segments1. The systematic methodology relies on five critical strategic evaluation dimensions: Regulatory Compulsion Index: This dimension measures whether the customer's purchase is discretionary or driven by immediate, non-discretionary legislative mandates1. Segments facing hard regulatory compliance deadlines (such as India's upcoming heavy vehicle safety standards or Saudi Arabia's tracking laws) are prioritized because they exhibit condensed sales cycles and low marketing friction4. Technical Integration & Certification Friction: This parameter evaluates the engineering hours, architectural modifications, and safety homologation testing (such as ISO 26262 functional safety, AIS-004 electromagnetic compatibility, and AIS-189 cybersecurity certifications) required to design DeepGrid's silicon into the customer's platform7. Higher integration complexity delays time-to-revenue and increases cash burn1.

units.title: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
units.text: Price Elasticity & BOM Limit: This dimension analyzes the customer's tolerance for hardware acquisition costs1. Large commercial transport fleets and logistics networks in emerging markets exhibit extreme price sensitivity and thin operational margins, making them highly receptive to DeepGrid's projected low-cost ASIC board Bill of Materials (BOM) of , compared to expensive foreign imported computing systems costing upwards of 1. Sales Cycle & Time-to-Revenue Duration: This metric measures the duration between initial technical engagement and commercial volume shipments1. Direct passenger vehicle OEM sales cycles typically span three to five years, whereas off-highway industrial projects or defense research contracts often finalize procurement in under six to twelve months1. Operational Design Domain (ODD) Entropy: This dimension maps the physical environments of the application, contrasting highly structured, predictable interstate highways with unstructured, chaotic urban roadways and off-highway terrains1. High-entropy environments require real-world, localized training datasets that can process unique local variables (such as three-wheelers, unlit vehicles, and wandering livestock), which provides a natural moat against general-purpose global computing platforms1.

units.title: Actionable Recommendations: The Pre-Series A VC Investment Thesis
units.text: For venture capitalists evaluating DeepGrid Semi against global autonomy platforms and domestic semiconductor design startups, the investment thesis is built on three core strategic pillars1: Eliminating the "Hardware Squeeze Zone" via Vertical Integration: Software-only autonomous vehicle startups are structurally squeezed by high third-party hardware costs, as they are forced to purchase expensive merchant silicon compute engines to run their algorithms1. By executing complete vertical integration—designing its own ASIC, integrated radar DSP, and physical compute system—DeepGrid avoids this margin squeeze, capturing both premium hardware margins and high-margin recurring SaaS software revenue1. De-Risking Early Cash-Burn via the Dual-Use Tactical Wedge: DeepGrid is not a pre-revenue startup burning cash while waiting for long-horizon passenger vehicle OEM contracts to mature1. By deploying its currently functional FPGA platforms directly into tactical defense projects and port AGV environments, DeepGrid generates immediate, high-margin contract cash-flow1. This dual-use strategy provides vital operational validation data, cushions the startup's burn rate, and builds physical proof-of-concept traction to de-risk the TSMC tape-out phase1.

units.text: Capital Efficiency via Sovereign Compliance and Mature Nodes: While foreign incumbents burn hundreds of millions of dollars attempting to design chips on expensive FinFET nodes1, DeepGrid's utilization of TSMC's mature HPC+ node represents an extremely capital-efficient engineering path1. In summary, DeepGrid's GTM strategy intelligently adapts the dual-use pragmatism of Kodiak and the constrained-environment focus of Gatik to the unique regulatory landscape of India and the GCC1. Funding DeepGrid is a calculated bet that aggressive vertical integration on a mature node is the only economically viable method to capture the impending, mandate-driven commercial vehicle safety and autonomy market1.
